title: Wesley So Has Taken the Lead at Norway Chess. All Four Indian Players Lost in Round Six.
excerpt: Gukesh fell to Keymer, Praggnanandhaa lost to So, Divya was beaten by Ju Wenjun, and Humpy lost in Armageddon. Carlsen exacted revenge on Firouzja to climb off the bottom.
body:
It was the worst day of the tournament for Indian chess. In round six of Norway Chess 2026 in Oslo, all four Indian competitors — Gukesh Dommaraju, R. Praggnanandhaa, Divya Deshmukh, and Koneru Humpy — suffered defeats, and the tournament's dynamics shifted dramatically.

Wesley So, the Filipino-American grandmaster, took over the lead with a clinical classical victory over Praggnanandhaa. It was Pragg's second consecutive loss after his round five defeat to Gukesh, and it dropped the 20-year-old to the bottom half of the standings.

So's win came a day after he had taken down Magnus Carlsen. Two classical wins in back-to-back rounds is the kind of surge that transforms a tournament, and the American veteran now leads with 11.5 points, 1.5 clear of Alireza Firouzja.

## Carlsen's Revenge, Firouzja's First Loss

The most symbolic result of the round came on the top board. Carlsen, who had been in last place and had lost 16 Elo points in five rounds, beat Firouzja in classical play to exact revenge for his opening-round defeat. It was Firouzja's first classical loss of the tournament.

The victory pulled Carlsen to 7.5 points — no longer last — and ended Firouzja's aura of invincibility. The Iranian-born French grandmaster had dominated the first five rounds, winning two classical games and never losing one. That changed on a single afternoon.

## Keymer's Breakthrough Against the World Champion

The other decisive classical result was perhaps the most significant for its implications. Vincent Keymer, the 22-year-old German, defeated world champion Gukesh in his first win of the event — not just his first classical win, but his first win of any kind, including Armageddon.

Gukesh had entered round six on the back of his exhilarating round-five victory over Praggnanandhaa, which had felt like a turning point. Instead, the momentum evaporated. Keymer now sits in third place on eight points, having leapfrogged both Indian players in the open section.

The world champion remains on 6.5 points, unchanged from where he stood after beating Pragg, while Praggnanandhaa has slipped to six points and last place.

## Standings After Round 6

Wesley So leads on 11.5 points. Firouzja is second on 10. Keymer has climbed to third on 8. Carlsen is fourth on 7.5. Gukesh is fifth on 6.5. Praggnanandhaa is last on 6.

## Divya Loses to Ju Wenjun, Assaubayeva Regains the Lead

The women's tournament was equally punishing for India. Divya Deshmukh, who had taken the sole lead after round five with a brilliant classical win over Zhu Jiner, was beaten in classical play by Women's World Champion Ju Wenjun.

Ju had lost five consecutive Armageddon games before this round. Her classical victory over Divya — a thriller that vindicated her patient approach — was a reminder that the former champion remains dangerous when the games are long.

Bibisara Assaubayeva of Kazakhstan took advantage, beating Humpy in Armageddon to regain the sole lead. Humpy, the veteran Indian grandmaster, continues to struggle at the bottom of the women's standings.

Anna Muzychuk sits half a point behind Divya in third, after Zhu Jiner lost in Armageddon.

## What It Means for NRI Chess Fans

As IM Tania Sachdev observed on the broadcast, it was simply a sad day for Indian chess. Four players, four losses. The kind of round that makes you check the calendar to see if it was some cosmic alignment.

But the tournament is not over. Round seven begins on Monday, June 1, at 8:30 PM IST. Gukesh is 5 points behind the leader with three rounds to play, which makes a title challenge virtually impossible. The battle now is for pride, for rating points, and for the kind of form that matters ahead of the World Championship defence later this year.

For Divya, the situation is more promising. She trails Assaubayeva by just 1.5 points and has already shown she can win classical games in this field. The final three rounds will define whether her Norway Chess debut is remembered as a near-miss or a breakthrough.
author: Diaspora Desk
